title: Special characters
subtitle: Bash meta-characters — flip to reveal meaning and how they differ

cards.notes: From # to end of line is not executed. Exception: #! on line 1 is the sha-bang, not a comment.

cards.example: echo one; echo two; echo three
cards.notes: Runs commands in sequence on one line. Status of the line = last command. Not the same as &&.

cards.example: case "$1" in start) echo starting ;; esac
cards.notes: One ; separates commands. Two ;; close a case arm.
Runs a file in the current shell (same idea as source). Space required after the dot. Variables stay.
No space: path in the current directory. Contrast with ". file" (source). Also .hidden and .. (parent).
Groups into one word. $, backticks, and \ still work inside.
Everything literal — no $ expansion, no backticks.
All expressions run; the value is the last one (here a=9, t2=5).
Next character is literal, or join lines if \ is last on the line.
Runs the command and is replaced by its output. Same job as $(…).
Does nothing, status 0 (like true). Not a semicolon. Useful as always-true while : ; do …; done.
Starts parameter/variable expansion (and $?, $1, $(…), …). The value of …, not the letters of the name.
